B039n.old: D-serine may help therapy update old memories, because it switches on a spot on the NMDA receptor that this kind of learning needs ([Wolosker, et al, 1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC23961)), and it may also open the GluD channels. The drug that's actually been tested with exposure therapy (facing the feared thing in small, safe doses) is a different one, D-cycloserine (DCS), which works on that same spot, and across 21 trials with over 1,000 patients it gave exposure therapy a small boost ([Mataix-Cols, et al, 2017](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/2599177)). It does not erase fear directly; it appears to strengthen whatever learning occurs during or after the exposure session. This is why session quality matters: if the exposure produces corrective learning and ends with reduced fear or mastery, DCS (and possibly D-serine also) may help consolidate that new memory; if the exposure is overwhelming or ends badly, it may consolidate the wrong association ([Smits, et al, 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3747985)).
B039n.new: D-serine may help therapy update old memories, since it switches on a spot on the NMDA receptor that this kind of learning needs ([Wolosker, et al, 1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC23961)). But the drug that's actually been tested alongside exposure therapy (facing the feared thing in small, safe doses) is a different one, D-cycloserine (DCS), which works on that same spot, and across 21 trials with over 1,000 patients it gave the therapy a small boost ([Mataix-Cols, et al, 2017](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/2599177)). So what does it actually do? It doesn't erase fear, it strengthens whatever you learn in the session, good or bad. End the session with the fear down and some sense of mastery, and DCS (and maybe D-serine) helps that stick; end it overwhelmed, and it can lock in the fear instead ([Smits, et al, 2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3747985)).

B040n.old: The Fix ("Lock, Stock, and Barrel"):The Brake (NAC): NAC gives the brain's support cells cystine (an amino acid), which they swap for glutamate, and in rat studies that glutamate outside the synapse trips a brake (the mGluR2/3 receptors) that cuts how much glutamate gets fired into the synapse ([Moran, et al, 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1413952)).
B040n.new: The Fix: The Brake (NAC): NAC gives the brain's support cells cystine (an amino acid), which they trade for glutamate, and in rats that glutamate sitting outside the synapse turns on a brake that cuts how much glutamate gets released into it ([Moran, et al, 2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1413952)).

B041n.old: The Lock (Zinc/Magnesium): Magnesium physically plugs the NMDA receptor's channel while the cell is at rest ([Jalali-Yazdi, et al, 2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6333211)), and zinc mostly makes the channel open less often, with a weaker plug of its own ([Amico-Ruvio, et al, 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21504727/)), so less of the voltage gets through.
